# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

## Regional Context: Physician Emigration Across North African Health Systems {#sec-intro-regional}

The escalating emigration of highly trained medical professionals from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) represents a profound structural challenge to the sustainability of national health systems, the achievement of Universal Health Coverage (UHC), and global health equity [@who2021; @sousa2023; @oecd2019]. Across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, the health workforce crisis has reached critical proportions, with physician outflows accelerating dramatically over the past decade [@elmorabety2022; @gouda2021; @sylla2021; @akl2008]. Middle-income North African health systems—historically characterized by strong public-sector traditions and high-standard university medical training—increasingly operate as uncompensated feeder systems for high-income destination countries facing domestic medical workforce shortages, most notably France and Germany [@drees2024; @bak2024; @oecd2019].

In neighboring Morocco, cross-sectional investigations indicate that over 70.1% of final-year medical students intend to emigrate immediately upon graduation [@sylla2021], driven by severe dissatisfaction with public hospital compensation (97.0%) and superior clinical working environments abroad (99.0%). Consequently, approximately one in three Moroccan-trained physicians currently practices in OECD nations, generating acute specialist shortages across provincial and rural district hospitals [@elmorabety2022]. Similarly, in Egypt, where economic devaluation and hospital budgetary constraints have severely eroded real physician earnings, nationwide surveys reveal that 89.6% of young medical practitioners report active migration intentions [@gouda2021]. In Lebanon, chronic macroeconomic instability and political fragility have driven over 67.0% of medical graduates toward overseas practice [@akl2008]. Across North Africa, national health systems share structural vulnerabilities: escalating patient loads, critical hospital infrastructure deficits, chronic shortages of essential pharmaceuticals and diagnostic consumables, low public-sector remuneration grids, and increasing exposure to physical and verbal workplace violence in acute care wards [@bensalem2024; @dhouib2024].

Within this regional landscape, Tunisia presents an exceptionally acute and policy-critical case study. Following independence in 1956, Tunisia established one of the most sophisticated public medical education and healthcare delivery infrastructures in Africa [@ms2023; @ins2024]. Four state faculties of medicine—located in Tunis, Sousse, Monastir, and Sfax—were established to train a competent cadre of primary care physicians, hospital-university faculty, and specialized clinicians. For decades, this domestic training pipeline successfully supplied the national health service (*Santé Publique*), underpinning remarkable public health achievements and demographic transitions.

However, the macroeconomic and institutional shocks following the 2011 revolution—further aggravated by the fiscal strain of the COVID-19 pandemic and post-2021 economic stagnation—have triggered an unprecedented exodus of medical personnel [@benromdhane2022; @dhouib2024]. Recent empirical microdata document that 68.6% of young Tunisian physicians and 75.6% of medical residents express concrete intentions to emigrate [@benromdhane2022; @dhouib2024]. Concurrently, administrative registries from the National Council of the Order of Physicians (*Conseil National de l'Ordre des Médecins*, CNOM) demonstrate a dramatic inflection: requests for certificates of good standing (*attestations de bonne conduite*)—the mandatory administrative clearance required for overseas licensing—rose from an average of 500–700 per year between 2015 and 2020 to more than 1,450 in 2024 alone, totaling over 6,000 requests between 2021 and 2024 (\~10% of the national practicing stock) [@cnom2025]. Official destination registries in France (DREES/RPPS) and Germany (Bundesärztekammer) corroborate this surge, confirming that Tunisian-trained practitioners represent one of the fastest-growing foreign non-EU medical cohorts in Western Europe [@drees2024; @bak2024].

## Theoretical Foundations: WHO Health Labour Market Framework and Push-Pull Dynamics {#sec-intro-framework}

To model these complex workforce dynamics without relying on arbitrary behavioral assumptions or overly simplistic single-factor theories, this study grounds its architecture in two established theoretical pillars:

1.  **The WHO Health Labour Market Framework (HLMF)**: The World Health Organization conceptualizes health workforce dynamics not as static supply-demand equilibria, but as an interconnected, multi-stage pipeline [@who2021]. As formalized in @fig-conceptual-framework, the HLMF models the complete lifecycle of health personnel: from medical education admission (*numerus clausus*), undergraduate and postgraduate curriculum progression, and board certification, to domestic labor market entry, inter-sectoral reallocation between public hospitals and private practice, internal rural-to-urban geographic transfers, international emigration, diaspora return migration, and statutory retirement exits [@who2021; @sousa2023].
2.  **Push-Pull Migration Theory and the Macro-Meso-Micro Determinant Taxonomy**: Rooted in classical migration economics [@mejia1978; @kline2003] and comprehensively synthesized across 107 global health workforce studies by @sousa2023, health worker mobility is propelled by the interplay of multi-level domestic push factors and international pull incentives:
    - **Macro-level drivers**: National economic conditions, inflation, currency depreciation, health budget allocations, and health sector governance.
    - **Meso-level drivers**: Hospital infrastructure quality, availability of medical equipment and consumables, bed-to-doctor ratios, on-call remuneration, academic supervision in university hospitals, and physical workplace security [@benromdhane2022; @bensalem2024; @dhouib2024].
    - **Micro-level drivers**: Individual career stage (resident vs. mid-career vs. senior), clinical specialty cluster (general practice vs. cognitive medical vs. surgical/critical care), and familial ties.
    - **International pull factors**: Substantial cross-border wage disparities (400% to 700% higher in Western Europe and the Gulf), structured post-graduate specialization pathways, streamlined foreign credentialing pathways (such as the French *Praticiens à diplôme hors Union Européenne* \[PADHUE\] *Épreuves de Vérification des Connaissances* \[EVC\] and German *Approbation*), and superior quality of life [@drees2024; @bak2024; @oecd2019].

## Methodological Vulnerabilities in Existing Workforce Studies {#sec-intro-gaps}

Despite the evident policy urgency, previous health workforce analyses in North Africa have predominantly relied on static headcount projections or unadjusted intention surveys. These approaches suffer from four major methodological vulnerabilities:

1.  **The Intention-to-Action Realization Gap**: Stated migration intentions in surveys measure latent willingness rather than realized physical migration. Multi-country econometric panels demonstrate that only 25% to 45% of skilled individuals expressing strong migration intentions actually realize international departures within a 3–5 year window, constrained by destination licensing quotas, visa barriers, language requirements, and personal inertia [@clemens2020; @docquier2014; @creighton2013]. Applying unadjusted intention rates directly to simulation models causes catastrophic and mathematically spurious workforce collapses within single five-year windows.
2.  **Non-Collapsibility of Survey Odds Ratios**: Stated preference surveys frequently report odds ratios (ORs) from multivariable logistic regressions (e.g., $\text{OR} = 2.14$ for salary dissatisfaction [@benromdhane2022] or $\text{OR} = 2.06$ for workplace violence [@dhouib2024]). In high-prevalence settings where baseline intention exceeds 70%, odds ratios diverge substantially from relative risks (RRs). Directly applying cross-sectional ORs as multiplicative risk ratios severely overstates policy elasticity due to the mathematical non-collapsibility of the odds ratio [@zhang1998].
3.  **Inframarginal Public Wage Bill Expansion**: In health economics, retention policies involving salary raises cannot be restricted solely to the marginal fraction of physicians contemplating emigration; statutory civil service agreements mandate wage scale expansions across all currently employed public physicians [@sanders2016; @drummond2015]. Costing interventions solely on marginal retained doctors underestimates government fiscal outlays by more than 90%.
4.  **Net Human Capital Valuation**: Emigration models that treat gross medical education costs as pure deadweight loss overlook the substantial volume of frontline clinical care delivered by medical residents during their 4–5 years of postgraduate hospital training, which offsets a substantial portion of university training expenditures [@sanders2016].

## Study Objectives {#sec-intro-objectives}

To overcome these methodological vulnerabilities, this study develops a parsimonious, structurally identified, and empirically calibrated dynamic cohort simulation model and economic evaluation of physician emigration from Tunisia over a mandatory 25-year horizon (2025–2050, spanning 2020–2050 total simulation time).

The primary research objective is: \> *What are the long-term workforce, spatial equity, and fiscal consequences of physician emigration from Tunisia, and which feasible retention, infrastructure, training, and regional policies maximize retained physician-years while optimizing public spending through 2050?*

Specifically, the study aims to:

1\. Model the baseline 30-year trajectory (2020–2050) of Tunisia's total, public-sector, private-sector, and regional physician stock under the continuation of post-2021 emigration rates (Status Quo).

2\. Quantify how multi-attribute working conditions, financial remuneration, regional hardship, and specialty credentialing hurdles translate into realized physical emigration flows.

3\. Simulate five targeted and bundled retention policy counterfactuals spanning public wage adjustments, hospital infrastructure modernization, regional hardship allowances, training quota expansion, and comprehensive reform.

4\. Conduct a public payer Cost-Consequence Analysis (CCA) and Budget Impact Analysis (BIA) compliant with CHEERS 2022 standards [@husereau2022], estimating incremental cost-effectiveness ratios ($\text{ICER}_{\text{public}}$ and $\text{ICER}_{\text{interior}}$) per discounted physician-year retained.

5\. Evaluate decision uncertainty and policy robustness through deterministic one-way sensitivity analysis and a 1,000-draw Monte Carlo Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA).
